Prevention: Grow maize rows around tomato fields to attract the winged flying aphids out of the tomato field (not all are winged)
Avoid chemical sprays as they kill the natural enemies of aphids, which are often able to suppress aphid populations, particularly at the end of the season.
Monitoring: Search for tiny soft, roundish insects on the underside of leaves or on stems.
They can be whitish, green, yellowish, brown or black.
A single aphid is almost too small to see, but groups of aphids can be seen.
Aphids produce sticky liquids that cover leaves and stems (called honey dew), which attracts ants.
When 5 to 10 plants per 50 m2 field have each at least few leaves full of aphids, then consider action.
When tomato viruses are known to be in the area, then act earlier, because aphids transmit viruses.
Direct Control: Stir 3 tablespoons liquid soap with 4 litres water.
Spray every week as long as justified by the monitoring results.
Fill container ½ with marigold (Tagetes) and cover with water.
Let it stand and ferment 5-10 days with occasional stirs, then strain, add double water.
Neem extract a maximum of 3 times (2.5-3 litres/ha or 50-60 ml /20 litres water; or 20 – 50 g neem seed cake or seed powder / litre water).
Ferment cow urine in a drum for 14-21 days (may add cow dung to make slurry), filter; mix with water 1:14.
Finely shop 20 garlic cloves, soak 1 day in 100 ml mineral oil, then add 10 ml soap, stir, add 2 litre water, stir.
Spray over plants a max of 2 x in min 7 day interval.
Sprays must cover the aphids, otherwise they will not work.
Restrictions: Green measures are usually enough to control aphids, and no chemicals are needed.
Only in rare cases of heavy aphid infestation or in cases of tomato virus occurrence in the area, you may consider sprays.
Do not spray on fruiting plants.
When using a pesticide, always wear protective clothing and follow the instructions on the product label.
